bollymeter.basis: A 98% RT score from 53 critics is near-unanimous: Mark Rylance's Cromwell is a performance for the ages, internalising power rather than performing it, and Peter Kosminsky's direction treats Tudor intrigue as genuine moral horror.

seasons.review_body: Wolf Hall's six-episode first season broadcast on BBC Two from January 2015 and became the defining prestige drama of that year in British television. The 98-percent Rotten Tomatoes score from 53 critics reflected a rare near-consensus: adapting Hilary Mantel's novels should have been unfilmable, and Peter Kosminsky delivered something very close to their true weight. The Guardian called it sumptuous, intelligent, event television. Mark Rylance plays Cromwell as a man who thinks in silence, whose stillness is itself a form of dominance - the performance resists every convention of the scheming-courtier archetype. Claire Foy's Anne Boleyn is equally startling: volatile, strategic, and finally tragic. The six-episode discipline imposed Mantel's moral seriousness without the sprawl that ruins historical adaptations.

episode_reviews.title: Three Card Trick
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The premiere establishes Cromwell's world obliquely - we enter through Cardinal Wolsey's fall rather than Cromwell's rise, and the show's distinctive grammar of silences and sidelong looks is immediately apparent. Rylance says very little; everything is communicated in the gap between what is said and what is decided. Damian Lewis as Henry VIII arrives like weather rather than like a king.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Cromwell at Wolsey's deathbed - loyalty held without sentiment, the quiet establishment of what this man is actually made of.
episode_reviews.review_body:
# Wolf Hall S1E1: "Three Card Trick" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

**Wolsey** is told he is out before the hour has warmed its hands. The King's orders arrive as fact, and the room starts rearranging itself around that fact. Then **Cromwell** asks for paper. Not feeling, loyalty, or outrage. Paper. That is the episode's cleanest move: power enters like a command, but it has to survive procedure. "Three Card Trick" makes Tudor politics feel less like a thunderclap than a legal bottleneck, then waits for the domestic illness sequence to show what happens when control has no document to hide behind.

## A Fall Measured in Paper

The opener understands that a dismissal can be more violent when nobody raises a sword. Wolsey is acted upon from the first beat, named, notified, and reduced by the phrase that matters: the King's orders. The force does not need volume. Wolsey's status can be altered by someone else's instruction.

What keeps the scene from playing as simple humiliation is Wolsey's own contradiction. He frames everything he has as coming from the King, which is meant to protect him. If his house, office, shelter, and standing all derive from royal favor, then he can still imagine himself inside the circle of power. The episode lets that logic curdle. The same dependence that once gave him height now makes his fall easy to administer.

York Place sharpens the point. Wolsey debates taking it, insisting on the King's role in what he owns and what he can claim. The writing is interested in the awful etiquette of decline: a man trying to convert dependency into legitimacy while the machinery around him has already started moving. The episode's thesis lands early. In this world, authority is recognition, paperwork, timing, and who gets to say the King's name first.

## Cromwell Makes Procedure Bite

Cromwell's entrance is a whisper, then a blockage. He does not storm the scene. He inserts a requirement. If the Seal is to be surrendered, a written request is necessary. If the Master of the Rolls is not there, the process cannot simply glide forward. The show turns legal form into drama, which is a harder trick than shouting about stakes.

This is the hour's sharpest characterization of Cromwell. He wants the proceedings moving, but he refuses to let them move on sloppy authority. That tension gives him shape. He is not simply loyal to Wolsey, and he is not clever as decoration. He understands that the only way to resist a command from above is to make the command prove itself in the correct form.

The pacing in these early exchanges is fast, built from short replies and procedural turns. The effect is a courtly card game where the winning hand may be a missing signature. This is where "Three Card Trick" earns its title without underlining it. The deception is not theatrical. It sits inside rules everyone claims to respect until those rules become inconvenient.

The limitation is density. The episode front-loads a lot of institutional language before the emotional shape has settled. It is bracing, but austere. The hour trusts procedure so much that the feeling has to be reached through the paperwork.

## Rome Enters Through a Side Door

After the dismissal mechanics, the episode widens into the divorce and annulment question. The beat around sin and the return to Rome reframes Wolsey's fall as part of a larger pressure system. The King wants an answer. Rome controls the path. Reformist belief sits in the house like a flame that needs cover.

This is where Cromwell's private danger begins to matter. He wants Wolsey's backing as protection for reformist beliefs, but the hour has already made Wolsey's protection unstable. That is good plotting because the danger is not announced as a new threat. It grows out of the first scene. If the patron weakens, the household's ideas become easier to hunt.

The late arrival beat after drunken boatmen also does more than provide period texture. It punctures the courtly machinery with ordinary inconvenience. Men can argue law, Rome, sin, and royal will, and still be delayed because the boatmen were drunk. The hour has a dry sense of scale. History may be grinding forward, but transport remains transport.

The episode's middle stretch does not chase easy momentum. It lets ideology and logistics share the frame. That choice can make the hour feel talk-heavy, but it defines the show's battlefield. Here, a household conversation can carry the same danger as an official summons.

## The Bedside Breaks the Courtly Rhythm

The illness sequence changes the grammar. Early scenes move through clipped legal obstacles. The bedside beat moves through repetition, plea, and panic. The appeal to open one's eyes is the episode's emotional break, and it works because the hour has spent so long showing Cromwell inside systems of control.

This is the first time procedure has no useful answer. No Seal problem can be delayed. No Master of the Rolls can be summoned. No royal phrasing can create authority over the body. The scene peaks through desperation, and the repetition matters. It strips the dialogue down from law to need.

The placement is crucial. If the hour opened with domestic anguish, it might have played as familiar tragedy. Coming after the Seal, York Place, Rome, reformist danger, and court timing, it lands as a rupture. The public world has rules, even when those rules are cruel. The private room has only waiting.

This is where the episode finds its pulse. Before this, "Three Card Trick" is intelligent and controlled. In the illness passage, the control cracks, and the earlier restraint pays off. The hour does not need to explain what the loss means for the household. It shows how quickly the language of power becomes useless beside a bed.

## Brighter Paint, Darker Room

The final instruction to brighten the painting is a clever last note because it returns the episode to surfaces. After illness, dismissal, and legal pressure, the command is administrative, ritual, almost absurdly practical. Make the image brighter. Arrange the visible world. Adjust what can still be adjusted.

That ending fits the hour's larger argument. People here survive by managing appearances, documents, houses, seals, punctuality, and portraits. The danger is that the management never stops the damage. It can only shape how the damage is seen.

The episode also plants its season cleanly. Wolsey's fall will not remain a private disgrace. It touches the King's struggle with Rome, Cromwell's place in a reformist household, and the question of whether law can protect anyone when royal will has already moved. The hour does not overplay that setup. It trusts the opening wound to keep bleeding.

The complaint is that "Three Card Trick" can feel colder than its strongest scenes prove it to be. The craft is exact, but exactness delays warmth. Still, the coldness has a purpose. The episode teaches the rules of the table before it shows the cost of losing a hand.

## The Verdict

"Three Card Trick" is a controlled, intelligent opener that makes paperwork feel like combat and domestic crisis feel like the place where combat stops helping. Its best move is refusing to separate power from process. Wolsey's dismissal, Cromwell's legal obstruction, the annulment pressure, and the illness sequence all belong to the same argument: authority is fragile when it depends on recognition from someone else.

The episode is dense early, and the procedural texture will test patience before the emotional turn arrives. The payoff is strong. Cromwell emerges through action rather than announcement, Wolsey's fall carries immediate political weight, and the final image of brightness being ordered into place leaves a bitter aftertaste. For the season, the hour draws a clean line from the Seal to Rome to the reformers, with Cromwell standing where the pressure will gather.

verdict.one_liner: A sharp opener turns Tudor power into paperwork, then lets illness expose the cost behind Cromwell's controlled face.

episode_reviews.title: The Devil's Spit
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The episode serves as the season's pivot, with the political situation crystallising into something genuinely dangerous and Cromwell's manoeuvrings gaining moral weight he cannot put down. Foy's Boleyn in this episode is the show at its most tightly coiled.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The negotiation in the antechamber where the question of what Cromwell will do next becomes genuinely uncertain for the first time.

bollymeter.basis: Nine years after Season 1, the continuation of Mantel's trilogy delivered on every expectation: Rylance's Cromwell is older, more powerful, and more doomed, and the season's direction under Kosminsky matches the first's cold elegance.

seasons.review_body: Wolf Hall: The Mirror and the Light aired on BBC One from November 2024, nine years after the first season, adapting the final volume of Hilary Mantel's trilogy about Thomas Cromwell's rise and fall under Henry VIII. Rylance returned with the same quality of inward performance, now aged into a Cromwell who has accumulated power and enemies in roughly equal measure. The season maintained the visual grammar established in 2015 - candlelight, compressed space, conversations that say everything through what is withheld. It tracked Cromwell's trajectory from royal architect to condemned man with the same emotional restraint that made the first season a landmark. Audience IMDb ratings held at 8.6 per episode. The nine-year wait did not diminish the show's authority.
seasons.season_over_season: The continuation picks up the Cromwell arc at its zenith and builds steadily toward its historical conclusion; the emotional tone darkens without the show ever losing its moral precision.
